30-001.r: Formic acid (HCOOH) is a stronger acid than acetic acid (CH3COOH): acetic acid's electron-donating methyl group makes losing H+ harder. Both are organic acids.

30-002.r: HOOC–COOH → oxalic acid (ethanedioic acid), the simplest dicarboxylic acid; found in many vegetables and plants; stronger than acetic acid.

30-003.r: Muscle fatigue after long hard work → accumulation of lactic acid in the muscles; rest (and massage) relieves it.

30-006.r: Lemon's sourness → citric acid (up to 8% of dry weight in lemons and limes). Vinegar → acetic acid; tamarind → tartaric acid.

30-008.r: Lactic acid → milk; acetic acid → vinegar; citric acid → lemon; butyric acid → rancid butter.

30-010.r: Not matched: acetic acid – potato (acetic acid → vinegar; potato has citric, oxalic, malic acids). Correct: lactic acid – curd; tartaric acid – grapes.

30-011.r: Wrong pair: lactose – sour milk → sour milk has lactic acid (from fermented lactose, the milk sugar). Correct: carbonic acid – soda water; formic acid – red ants.

30-012.r: Wrong pair: acetic acid – curd → curd has lactic acid. Correct: ascorbic acid (vitamin C) – lemon; maltose – malt; formic acid – red ant (and bee stings).

30-013.r: Pickle → acetic acid; sour milk → lactic acid; apple → malic acid; cold drinks and soda water → carbonic acid.

30-014.r: Vinegar → acetic acid; tamarind → tartaric acid; sour milk/curd → lactic acid; nettle sting → methanoic (formic) acid.

30-015.r: Wrong pair: souring of milk – nitric acid → lactic acid sours milk. Correct: vinegar – acetic acid; bones – calcium phosphate; gastric juice – hydrochloric acid.

30-016.r: Milk left open turns sour → lactic acid; lactobacillus bacteria ferment lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid.

30-018.r: Milk → curd: lactobacillus bacteria (at about 30-40°C) convert lactose into lactic acid, giving the sour taste; curd making is a bacterial biotechnological process.

30-020.r: Predominant organic acid in grapes → tartaric acid, a white crystalline diprotic acid.

30-021.r: Tomatoes → rich in citric acid (with malic acid); oxalic acid only in small amounts.

30-022.r: Acid abundant in grapes, tamarind and banana → tartaric acid; used in food as regulator and antioxidant.

30-023.r: Acid used in photography → oxalic acid. Formic acid → ants; citric acid → lemon; acetic acid → vinegar.

30-024.r: Baking powder → tartaric acid combined with baking soda as a leavening agent; tartaric acid is also a main acid in wine.

30-025.r: Odour of acetic acid (CH3COOH) → like vinegar; vinegar is mainly acetic acid and water.

30-026.r: Vinegar → solution of acetic acid (ethanoic acid, CH3COOH), which gives its sour taste and pungent smell; made by fermenting ethanol.

30-028.r: Vinegar → acetic acid (CH3COOH) + water; acetic acid bacteria ferment ethanol (from sugarcane juice, molasses); used in cooking and as a preservative.

30-032.r: Glycine (NH2CH2COOH) → not optically active: its central carbon carries 2 hydrogen atoms, so no carbon has four different groups. Alanine and serine are optically active.

31-001.r: Most explosions in mines → methane + air mixture; methane is explosive at about 5–15% in air.

31-002.r: Not an explosive → nitrochloroform (chloropicrin): a fungicide, herbicide, insecticide and tear gas (poison gas in World War I). TNT, trinitroglycerine and RDX are explosives.

31-004.r: 'Nobel oil' → trinitroglycerin (TNG), an explosive fluid (an organic nitrate).

31-005.r: RDX (Research Department Explosive, cyclonite) → discovered by George Friedrich Henning of Germany, patented 1898; used from World War II.

31-006.r: Correct statement: RDX is an explosive → cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine, also called cyclonite, hexogen, T4; more powerful than TNT, widely used in World War II.
31-006.t: TNT and RDX are explosives, not insecticides.

31-008.r: HMX → High Melting Explosive (octogen), a powerful, relatively insensitive nitroamine explosive related to RDX.
31-008.c: The book calls HMX a colourless liquid; HMX is a colourless crystalline solid.

31-009.r: CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 → all explosives in military weapons; CL-20 and HMX are also rocket/missile propellants, LLM-105 purely a military explosive.

31-010.r: Explosive → nitroglycerine: heavy, colourless, oily liquid; also called trinitroglycerol (TNG) or glyceryl trinitrate (GTN).

31-011.r: No nitroglycerine → amatol (ammonium nitrate + TNT); cordite, blasting gelatine and dynamite all contain nitroglycerine.

31-012.r: Glycerol + conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 → nitroglycerin (glyceryl trinitrate, Nobel's oil), used in explosives such as dynamite.

32-001.r: Natural fuel → petroleum (formed from fossils inside the Earth); coke and tar come from destructive distillation, coal gas is made artificially.

32-002.r: Cleanest fossil fuel → natural gas; gives less carbon and other emissions than coal and other fossil fuels.

32-003.r: Fossil fuels → coal, oil and natural gas, formed from organic matter over millions of years; finite. Alcohol, ether and water gas are not fossil fuels.

32-004.r: Highest fuel (calorific) value → hydrogen, about 150,000 kJ/kg; used as rocket fuel.

32-005.r: Indian coal power plants: many coastal ones use seawater (e.g. Mundra, Gujarat); about 48% are in water-scarce districts (CSE 2021); private ones exist (Adani Power) → none correct.

32-006.r: All correct: coal ash has arsenic, lead, mercury; coal plants emit sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides; Indian coal has high ash (25 to 45%, imported 10 to 20%).

32-007.r: Coal gasification (syngas) → can give ethanol and urea (via ammonia); not nitroglycerine, which comes from nitrating glycerin → only two.

32-008.r: Copper smelting concerns → sulfur dioxide emission and slag that leaches heavy metals (arsenic, lead, cadmium, nickel); not lethal carbon monoxide → 2 and 3.

32-009.r: Maximum indoor chemical pollution (among mosquito coil, coal, cooking gas, room spray) → burning coal.

32-010.r: Coke in a blast furnace → fuel that supplies heat and reducing agent that removes oxygen from iron oxide (as CO and CO2) → statements 1, 3.
32-010.t: Coke is a reducing agent, not an oxidizing agent.

32-011.r: Furnace oil → residue of crude oil distillation (refinery product); used for power generation in boilers, ships, industry; its sulfur causes SOx emissions → all 3 correct.

32-012.r: Both wrong: fuel from plastic waste has HIGH octane rating (lead-free 'green fuel'); HIGHER octane number = more compression withstood without detonating.

32-013.r: Octane number → quality of petrol: antiknock quality compared with iso-octane; higher octane number = better anti-knocking.
32-013.t: Octane number → petrol; cetane number → diesel.

32-015.r: Octane booster → tetraethyl lead (reduced knocking); it is no longer added to normal motor petrol, unleaded octane-boosters are used now.

32-016.r: Anti-knocking agent in petrol → tetraethyl lead (TEL); its lead forms lead oxide (PbO), stopping the fuel mixture from burning too quickly.

32-018.r: Cetane number → quality parameter of diesel (as octane number is for petrol); diesel ignites by compression, no spark.

32-019.r: Diesel engine fuel → diesel vapour + air; ignition comes from the heat of highly compressed air, with no spark or carburettor.
32-019.c: The book says the compressed air reaches about 80°F; that is roughly room temperature. Compression actually makes the air hot enough to ignite diesel.

32-020.r: Cooking gas (as asked) → methane, the chief component of biogas (gobar gas) used at home.

32-021.r: Fuel gas from a biogas plant → methane; methane is also the main component of natural gas.

32-022.r: Biogas (anaerobic breakdown of organic matter) → mainly methane (about 50%-70%) and carbon dioxide (about 30%-50%); small hydrogen sulfide and moisture.

32-027.r: Biogas (gobar gas) plant → works by fermentation of cattle dung and other wastes.

32-028.r: The book gives no single answer (*): the first gobar gas pilot plant was designed by S.V. Desai at IARI, New Delhi, in 1941-42.
32-028.t: The option names 'C.B. Desai'; the book's name is S.V. Desai.

32-029.r: Gas from rice fields → methane (CH4), a potent greenhouse gas made by anaerobic bacteria in flooded soil; also small amounts of nitrous oxide.

32-030.r: LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas) → hydrocarbons of 3-4 carbons: mainly butane (about 65%) and propane (about 35%), small ethane; main constituent butane.

32-035.r: Indane gas (LPG) → mixture of butane and propane.

32-036.r: LPG leak smell → ethyl mercaptan, added because LPG (butane + propane) is itself odourless.
32-036.t: The smell is not from butane or propane.

32-037.r: CNG → methane, ethane; LPG → butane, propane; coal gas → hydrogen, methane, carbon monoxide; water gas → carbon monoxide + hydrogen.

32-038.r: A false: LPG is mainly propane and butane, not methane. R true: methane (e.g. in biogas) can be burnt directly and piped to homes and factories.

32-039.r: No pressure gauge on domestic LPG cylinders → gas is stored as a liquid, so a gauge cannot show the quantity left.

32-041.r: Natural gas → mainly methane (CH4) with small amounts of higher alkanes; odourless; used as CNG and LNG.

32-043.r: CNG → Compressed Natural Gas: natural gas compressed to less than 1% of its volume at standard atmospheric pressure; alternative to petrol.

32-044.r: CNG (used in vehicles to cut pollution) → mainly methane (CH4), about 80% to 90%.

32-047.r: Only 1 true: LNG is natural gas (mainly methane) liquefied by cooling to about –162°C for storage/transport. India's first LNG terminal → Dahej, Gujarat, not Hassan.

32-048.r: Oxygen is absent in kerosene, a petroleum hydrocarbon mixture; glass, soil and cement contain oxygen.

32-049.r: Gasohol → petrol (gasoline) + ethyl alcohol (ethanol); higher octane, burns slowly, coolly and completely.

32-051.r: True: coal, petroleum, natural gas are fossil fuels; geothermal energy is non-conventional; gobar gas is mainly methane. False: gasohol is petrol + ethanol, not benzene.

32-052.r: Anti-freeze in automobile engines → ethylene glycol; it lowers the freezing point (and raises the boiling point) of the coolant.

32-053.r: Diesel in heavy vehicles → high power with economic saving; diesel engines are rugged, durable and fuel-efficient.

32-054.r: Carburettor (mixes air and fuel) → used in petrol engines, not diesel; largely replaced by fuel injection since the 1990s.

32-055.r: Catalytic converter catalysts → platinum, palladium and rhodium; they change harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.

32-056.r: Book's key for fuel efficiency → radial tyres (less rolling resistance), multipoint fuel injection, catalytic converter → 1, 3, 4.
32-056.c: Radial tyres, a streamlined body and fuel injection all save fuel, while a catalytic converter only cleans exhaust. No option gives 1, 2 and 3, so the book keeps (d) 'according to the options'.

32-057.r: Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF, low-carbon biofuel) feedstock → all four: agricultural residues, corn grain, wastewater sludge, wood mill waste.

32-058.r: Hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) → exhaust emits only water vapour (and warm air); no harmful tailpipe emissions.

32-059.r: Hydrogen fuel for vehicles → stored by absorbing it in a hydride (palladium hydride) at very low temperature; released by exhaust heat.

32-060.r: Petroleum refining by-product → asphalt (bitumen), sticky black viscous material; binder in road construction and used in waterproofing.

32-061.r: 'Hydrocarbon Vision 2025' → storage of petroleum products and long-term energy security via self-reliance (more domestic production, equity oil abroad).

33-001.r: Wax emulsion on fruits and vegetables → extends storage life (about 10 to 12 days); carries sprout inhibitors, growth regulators and preservatives.

33-002.r: Food (and fruit juice) preservative → sodium benzoate, sodium salt of benzoic acid, E number E211.

33-006.r: Food preservation → benzoic acid (simple aromatic carboxylic acid); its salts such as sodium benzoate are food preservatives.

33-007.r: Potato chips packed in nitrogen → prevents oxidation; without oxygen bacteria and moulds cannot grow, so shelf life is longer.

33-008.r: MSG (monosodium glutamate, 'Ajinomoto', sodium salt of glutamic acid) → flavour enhancer (umami) and preserver; book accepts both (b) and (c).

33-009.r: Fruits last longer in cold storage → respiration rate falls, so less ethylene ('fruit-ripening hormone') and slower ripening.

33-010.r: Refrigeration preserves food → slows biochemical reactions and the growth of microorganisms.
33-010.t: Refrigeration slows germs down; it does not kill them.

33-011.r: Domestic refrigerator refrigerant → Freon (DuPont trade name), a stable, mildly toxic halocarbon.

33-012.r: Triclosan (antibacterial chemical) → found in toiletries: antibacterial soaps, body washes, toothpastes, cosmetics; US FDA banned it in consumer antiseptic washes (2016).

33-013.r: Decolourising raw sugar → animal (bone) charcoal, used in sugar refining for filtration, decolourising and de-ashing.

33-014.r: Main component of honey → fructose (38.2%); glucose 31.3%, water 17.2%, maltose 7.1%, sucrose 1.3%.

33-015.r: Sweetest natural sugar → fructose (140-170 on a scale where sucrose = 100); glucose 70-80, maltose 30-50, lactose 20.

33-016.r: Invert sugar (sucrose hydrolysed into glucose + fructose) is sweeter than sucrose because of free fructose → A and R true, R not the explanation.

33-017.r: Grape sugar → glucose; fruit sugar → fructose; milk sugar → lactose; table sugar → sucrose; stevia → natural sweetener.

33-018.r: All four correctly matched: beet → sugar; honey → glucose and fructose; cotton → cellulose; milk → lactose.

33-019.r: Aspartame → about 200 times sweeter than sucrose; it gives four kcal per gram, but so little is needed that its calories are negligible.

33-020.r: Sweetness vs sucrose → alitame 2000 times (highest); sucralose 600; saccharin 200-700; aspartame 200.

33-021.r: Most useful classification of drugs in medicinal chemistry → by molecular targets (drug targets: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, nucleic acids).

33-022.r: Aspirin (a salicylate) → book: obtained from a tree; reduces pain, fever and inflammation; used against heart attacks and strokes.
33-022.c: Aspirin's tree link is willow bark, whose salicin led to it, not a 'latex tree'; aspirin itself is made by chemical synthesis from salicylic acid.

33-023.r: Aspirin → antipyretic (lowers fever) and analgesic (relieves pain).
